wealth.text:
The National Bank of Belgium's Household Finance and Consumption Survey found median household net wealth of €291,641 in Belgium at the end of 2024, well above the euro-area median of €152,480 — Belgian households are, on this measure, close to twice as wealthy as the euro-area typical household. Average wealth was around €555,000. Wealth is concentrated, but slightly less so than the euro-area average: the wealthiest 10% of Belgian households held 54.9% of net wealth (against the least wealthy 50% holding just 8.3%), giving a Gini coefficient of 68% — high, but below the euro area's 72%. Real estate makes up 59% of Belgian households' assets, reflecting a strong homeownership and property-investment culture.

On the institutional side, Belgium's insurance sector is a major source of household savings (see Insurance below, including its distinctive branch 21/branch 23 guaranteed-rate and unit-linked life products), while its funded occupational pension pillar remains comparatively modest — the identifiable segment data shows DB Pension (Corp) at $28.8bn against very small DC Pension (Corp) ($0.18bn) and DB Pension (Govt) ($0.14bn) figures, reflecting Belgium's continued reliance on its state PAYG pillar for the bulk of retirement provision, and a market where the insurance channel is the larger near-term opportunity.

sources.label: National Bank of Belgium, Press release - Distribution of household net wealth 2024-Q4
VRT NWS, With fortunes averaging 555,000 euro, households in Belgium are richer than in most other EU countries

pensions.text:
Belgium runs a three-pillar system broadly similar in structure to its neighbours, but with a state-dominated first pillar that still does most of the work. The first pillar, pension légale (legal pension), is a state PAYG scheme financed through social security contributions on employees' salaries. The second pillar, pension complémentaire (complementary pension), is employer-provided and genuinely funded (financed by capitalisation), delivered either through a group insurance contract with an insurer or through an OFP (organisme de financement des pensions, a dedicated pension financing institution) — the state actively encourages this pillar through tax and social-contribution reductions, and pension institutions face minimum guaranteed-return requirements depending on the type of plan. A voluntary third pillar of tax-advantaged individual pension and long-term savings sits on top.

The identifiable segment data shows Belgium's funded occupational pillar is still comparatively modest in scale: DB Pension (Corp), the largest segment at $28.8bn, is led by dedicated corporate schemes for Anheuser-Busch InBev ($3.9bn), KBC Group ($3.0bn) and ExxonMobil's Belgian operations ($2.8bn), alongside sectoral OFPs including Amonis (a fund for liberal professions such as doctors and pharmacists, $2.1bn), Pensioenfonds Metaal (the metal sector, $1.8bn) and Fluvius (the Flemish utility network operator, $1.7bn) — a well-identified shortlist of the largest institutional relationships in this market. DC Pension (Corp) and DB Pension (Govt) remain very small by comparison, at $0.18bn and $0.14bn respectively.

sources.label: FSMA, Quels sont les trois piliers de pension en Belgique?
CMS, Comprehensive Overview of Pensions in Belgium

insurance.text:
Assuralia (the Belgian insurance association) reported total premiums of €35.1 billion in 2024, up 8.4% on the prior year, with life premiums (€18.4bn) narrowly ahead of non-life (€16.7bn), a 52.4% life share. Life business is built substantially around two distinctive product branches: branch 21 (individual guaranteed-rate life insurance, a major and long-standing Belgian household savings vehicle, up 10.8% to €7.1bn in premiums in 2024) and branch 23 (unit-linked products, which surged 34.5% to €3.8bn on favourable equity markets).

The identifiable OECD-sourced segment figures — Life insurance $11.8bn and Non-life insurance $20.6bn — look notably small relative to Belgium's well-documented branch 21/23 life savings culture and premium volumes described above, and the unusual pattern of Non-life exceeding Life in these figures (the reverse of most European markets) suggests this segment may understate Belgium's true domestic life-insurance investment assets specifically. Worth treating as a caveat for sizing purposes: the branch 21/23 life savings market is likely a considerably larger opportunity than the identifiable figures alone suggest, and Assuralia's own membership is the more direct route to it.

sources.label: Becobra, Assuralia annual report 2025 - First reading of the figures
OECD, Asset allocation of insurance companies dataset (data-explorer.oecd.org)

charities.text: Belgium has no single national charity regulator comparable to England and Wales' Charity Commission. Belgian nonprofits mostly take the ASBL/VZW (association sans but lucratif / vereniging zonder winstoogmerk, non-profit association) legal form, with charitable foundations (fondations d'utilité publique/stichtingen van openbaar nut) covered separately below; no comprehensive, centrally-published aggregate financial figure for the broader ASBL/VZW association population was identified in available research. This population is best approached qualitatively for now; the King Baudouin Foundation, covered below, is the far better-documented and more significant institutional relationship in this market.

foundations.text:
Belgium's flagship philanthropic institution, the King Baudouin Foundation (KBF), is by some distance the largest public-utility foundation in the country. Established in 1976 to mark the 25th anniversary of King Baudouin's reign, KBF's 2024 annual accounts reported total assets of approximately €1.67 billion and equity of €1.60 billion, on operating income of €246.4 million; its 2025 operating budget was €220.3 million, funding more than 200 project calls a year and support for close to 5,000 organisations and individuals across health, poverty, culture, democracy, climate, education and international philanthropy.

Conventional institutional plan-sponsor classifications do not identify a matching population of Belgian foundation institutions comparable in scale to KBF, so no dedicated segment or asset-allocation chart is shown here — in any case, KBF's scale and its public-utility structure would not be well represented by that kind of classification, and it is best approached directly as a named institutional relationship.

sources.label: King Baudouin Foundation, Get to know the King Baudouin Foundation
Philanthropy.org, King Baudouin Foundation Belgium (financial data)

family_offices.text: No usable, internally-consistent single-family-office figures were identified for Belgium: 9 SFO-tagged firms appear in underlying data, but none carry a reliable figure. This significantly understates Belgium's real family-capital landscape. The AB InBev founding families (Van Damme, de Spoelberch and de Mévius) are collectively estimated to hold around €49.4 billion, Belgium's largest family fortune by a wide margin, though they run no single consolidated family office — the de Spoelberch and de Mévius families instead jointly operate the investment company Verlinvest, while the Spoelberch family separately co-invests with other wealthy families through Cogepa. The Colruyt family's investment vehicle, Korys, is estimated to manage around $4.5 billion, and the late Albert Frère's business empire (around €6.2bn) remains a significant, if now more dispersed, pool of Belgian family capital. None of these appear with a usable figure in available named-reporter data, meaning this segment represents a genuinely open relationship-building opportunity rather than a market that is already well covered.

sources.label: Percapita.be, The Most Economically Influential Families in Belgium
familyofficehub.io, Van Damme, De Spoelberch, De Mevius: Is there a Single Family Office?

sovereign_wealth_funds.text: Belgium's identifiable SWF segment ($10.6bn) is SFPI-FPIM (Société Fédérale de Participations et d'Investissement / Federale Participatie- en Investeringsmaatschappij), formally identified by Global SWF and the Sovereign Wealth Fund Institute as the Belgian sovereign wealth fund. Created in 2006 from the merger of Belgium's former Federal Participation Company and Federal Investment Company, SFPI-FPIM centrally manages the federal government's shareholdings while also pursuing its own investment policy on behalf of the Belgian economy — investing in companies (from SMEs to scale-ups) with strategic or social value, historically concentrated in life sciences, finance and aviation, and more recently expanding into energy, transport and impact investing. External reporting puts SFPI-FPIM's assets under management at around €14 billion on behalf of the federal state, somewhat above the identifiable $10.6bn segment figure here, likely reflecting timing and currency-conversion differences.

sources.label: FPS Finance, The Federal Holding and Investment Company

ocio.text:
No dedicated, regularly-published fiduciary management/OCIO market survey specific to Belgium was identified. Belgium's funded occupational pension pillar (discussed under Pensions above) is comparatively modest in scale, and many of the largest pools identified — dedicated single-employer schemes for AB InBev, KBC and ExxonMobil, and sectoral OFPs such as Amonis and Pensioenfonds Metaal — appear to be run through group insurance contracts or dedicated pension-financing institutions rather than delegated to an independent external fiduciary manager in the UK sense.

Globally, Cerulli estimates the OCIO/fiduciary management industry grew to more than $3.3 trillion in assets by the end of 2024, projecting growth to $5.6 trillion by the end of the decade — but Belgium's own share of that global pool isn't separately reported. The realistic route to delegated investment relationships in Belgium runs through the pension and insurance institutions named above.

sources.label: Cerulli Associates, Nearly $1.3 Trillion Expected to Flow into OCIO Industry Through 2029
